indicators.note: sound placed before the measure tells us to say that word and write what it sounds like

parts.note: quarts are units of liquid measure, two pints each

explanation.surface: A rock specimen found suspended in some fluid you can hear sloshing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective (healthy, solid) but is the homophone signal: quarts said out loud is spelt with a Z for the crystal.
explanation.definitionFit: A hard crystalline silica rock, common in sand and granite, classed as a mineral.

clue.text: Go-as-you-please tuneful medley, but classical please

definitions.meaning: a musical medley of tunes put together freely
Latin, the classical language, for 'what pleases'

explanation.surface: A request for a light musical medley, but please make it classical music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classical' means Latin here: quod libet is Latin for 'what you please'.
explanation.definitionFit: A light medley of well-known tunes; the name is Latin for whatever one likes.

parts.note: grazing livestock taken in on another person's land for a fee

explanation.surface: Pets put up at a boarding kennel.
explanation.walkthrough: To agist is to take in livestock to graze on your land for payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken in to graze on another's pasture for a fee, the legal term for livestock board.

parts.note: bureaucracy now demands every form be filled in three copies at least

explanation.surface: A complaint about how much paperwork is needed nowadays.
explanation.definitionFit: In three identical copies, which is how official forms seem always to be required.

parts.note: 'previously encountered' is 'met afore' in old or dialect speech, and the sound of that phrase is a figure of speech, which is what 'figuratively speaking' defines

explanation.surface: Someone recalls having met a person before, in a manner of speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure of speech that calls one thing by another's name, the core of figurative language.

parts.note: a governor is addressed as 'Your Excellency', and 'how splendid!' is an exclamation of praise

explanation.surface: A remark admiring the colonial governor.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation meaning very good, close to the governor's honorific Excellency.

clue.text: I'm fine though in a frenzy

parts.note: I'm is I am, with I dropped as in casual speech
OK means fine, all right

explanation.surface: Someone insists all is well while clearly losing control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'though' only links: 'I'm fine' gives AM OK.
explanation.definitionFit: Running wild in a violent frenzy, from the Malay word for a murderous rage.

parts.note: Pope's poem title, read literally as the cutting off of a lock of hair

explanation.surface: The title of Alexander Pope's mock-epic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: In Pope's poem the 'rape' is the snipping of a lock of Belinda's hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A trim at the barber's, the snipping of a lock of hair.

parts.note: a jumbo is an elephant, and one living solitary, apart from the herd, is the dangerous kind

explanation.surface: A very large flatfish.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue elephant lives alone away from the herd, so it is a solitary jumbo.

definitions.meaning: meat from cattle, bought at a butcher's shop

explanation.surface: A complaint made at the meat counter.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed solution's R is an OCR misreading of B: both definitions give the slang for a complaint, also the meat sold by a butcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a complaint, and also meat from cattle sold by butchers.

parts.note: 'cake-hole' is British slang for the mouth, which is one example of an opening in the body

explanation.surface: A question about a hole in a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cake-hole' is British slang for the mouth, so the clue asks for the general word of which the mouth is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouth is one bodily opening; the general word for any such opening is the answer.

clue.text: This time a hundred in defeat go dry

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
losing is suffering defeat

explanation.surface: A cricketer makes a hundred but still loses, and the bar shuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This time' is the time when pubs 'go dry': closing time, when the bar stops serving. 'in' only joins C to LOSING.
explanation.definitionFit: Pub closing time is the hour when drinks stop being served and the bar goes dry.

parts.note: the small inhabitants of fairyland, the elves and fairies, rather than small children

explanation.surface: Young children taken to a fairy-tale theme park.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional name for fairies and elves, the small people of folklore.

indicators.note: for read as 'converted for', telling us the letters of care are rearranged to stand for another word

explanation.surface: An instruction to look after the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is only 'for': the letters of CARE are turned into a unit of land.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of area used for measuring fields, so a measure of farmland.

clue.text: Poor old nag with a racing shoe no nails though

parts.note: a screw is slang for a worn-out horse
a plate is a light horseshoe used for racing

explanation.surface: A broken-down horse is shod with a racing shoe but no nails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' only links. The tool cuts screw threads, so it is for screws, not nails.
explanation.definitionFit: A steel plate for cutting threads on screws, a tool for screws rather than nails.

clue.text: R.A.F. type takes chilly refreshment in ladies' wear

parts.note: bod is RAF slang for a chap, a 'type'
ices are cold refreshments, ice creams

explanation.surface: An airman eats an ice cream while wearing women's clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'type' and 'bod' are both RAF-era slang for a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Close-fitting upper parts of women's dresses, a garment for women.

definitions.meaning: an adjective for the adverb answer: meant without guile, honestly
a subscription is a signature, and 'Yours ...' comes before it at the foot of a letter

explanation.surface: An honest foreword to a magazine subscription offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subscription' means the signature written below a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Honestly and without deceit; also the word after 'Yours' that precedes a letter's signature.

clue.text: Thrilled to be no longer in the position of co-respondent

parts.note: ex means former, no longer
a co-respondent in a divorce case is named, or cited, as the other party

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted not to be named any more in a divorce case.
explanation.walkthrough: A co-respondent is the person accused of adultery in a divorce suit, who is 'cited'; EX-CITED is someone no longer so named.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrilled and excited both mean stirred up with eager feeling.

clue.text: Original pottery from the Netherlands — careful now!

parts.note: Delft is the Dutch town where the pottery originated
'ware!' is an old warning cry meaning beware, take care

explanation.surface: Fragile Dutch pottery handled with a warning to be careful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ware!' is the old shout for 'beware', as in 'ware wire' on a hunting field.
explanation.definitionFit: Tin-glazed blue-and-white earthenware first made in a Dutch town, the original pottery of its kind.

clue.text: Stoke's location is transposed in New Jersey

indicators.note: transposed means the two parts of the place name swap ends

parts.note: Stoke-on-Trent is the English pottery town, so it is located on Trent

explanation.surface: A note that the Staffordshire town has been moved to America.
explanation.walkthrough: Stoke-on-Trent is an English city on the River Trent. 'is transposed' swaps ON and TRENT to give the capital of New Jersey.
explanation.definitionFit: The state capital of New Jersey, a city on the Delaware river.

definitions.meaning: a kind of mail or train, delivered or running quickly with few stops

explanation.surface: A quick postal train.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapid; also a type of quick delivery post or non-stopping train.

definitions.meaning: Arabella, daughter of the Dean of Barchester in Trollope's novel The American Senator, bears this surname
the plant genus of three-leaved clovers

explanation.surface: A young lady from a cathedral town is living in luxury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in clover' looks like the idiom for living comfortably; 'in' is only a link and clover is the second definition. Barchester is Trollope's fictional cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's Miss Arabella of that name is the Dean of Barchester's daughter, and the three-leaved plant genus shares the name.

clue.text: What do you think of the view ?

definitions.text: What do you think of the view ?

parts.words: What do you think of the view ?
parts.note: view here is a point of view; the question asks what one's own view is

explanation.surface: A tourist asks a companion's thoughts on the scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: A view in the sense of belief or judgment; what you think is your stance.

parts.note: the introduction to Blake's Songs of Innocence has a child asking the ... to play a song about a lamb

explanation.surface: A harmless tool belonging to someone called Blake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'innocent' points to William Blake's Songs of Innocence, whose opening poem is about a piper.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple wind instrument, played by the piper in Blake's introductory poem.

clue.text: The question may arise, are music and art on the increase?

definitions.text: The question may arise, are music and art on the increase?

parts.words: The question may arise, are music and art on the increase?
parts.note: one pops the question; pop is a kind of music and of art; up means on the increase; and the phrase means arise

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether interest in music and art is growing.
explanation.walkthrough: Each part points to the same phrase: 'pop the question', pop music, pop art, 'up' for increasing, and to arise suddenly.
explanation.definitionFit: To appear or arise suddenly, as a question might.

clue.text: A quibble from the French needlewoman?

definitions.text: A quibble from the French needlewoman?

parts.words: A quibble from the French needlewoman?
parts.note: a quibble is a petty point, and the French spelling of that phrase is a fine embroidery stitch a needlewoman would use

explanation.surface: A French seamstress raises a small objection.
explanation.definitionFit: Small diagonal tent stitch on canvas, an embroidery technique, whose name is French for small point.

clue.text: I am writing my last words to the naughty children

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm
a PS, postscript, is the last words written at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A dying parent writes a final message to unruly offspring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' only links. The surface suggests a deathbed letter, but the last words are a postscript.
explanation.definitionFit: Little devils, mischievous children.

definitions.meaning: a '... of Satan' is an old name for a mischievous child
an arm or leg of the body

explanation.surface: The Devil displays one of his legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'showing' only links. 'Limb of Satan' was a phrase for a little devil of a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the body such as an arm or leg; also the devil's agent in the phrase about a naughty child.

indicators.note: the letters of recipes are given in a new arrangement
form means a new shape for the letters, completing the rearrangement signal

explanation.surface: Cookery instructions written with exact measurements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given in ... form' tells us to put RECIPES into another form; the definition 'exact' sits inside the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Precise and exact both mean accurate in every detail.

clue.text: The court's decisions on capital reorganization

indicators.note: reorganization means the letters of capital are rearranged

explanation.surface: Judges rule on how a company's capital is to be restructured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reorganization' rearranges CAPITAL into a Latin plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin plural of placitum, legal term for judgments or decrees of a court.

parts.note: men of letters suggests writers, but here they are mail carriers, and trainee makes them boys

explanation.surface: Young apprentices learning to be writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Lads employed to carry mail, young messengers for the post office.

clue.text: His work has outlived its span over Father Thames

definitions.text: His work has outlived its span over Father Thames

parts.words: His work has outlived its span over Father Thames
parts.note: the engineer's London Bridge was taken down from the river and rebuilt in Arizona, outliving its span over the Thames

explanation.surface: A builder's achievement has lasted longer than it spanned the river.
explanation.walkthrough: John Rennie designed the London Bridge of 1831, sold in 1968 and moved to Arizona; 'span' is both the bridge and a length of time. The printed solution's B is an OCR misreading of R.
explanation.definitionFit: Scottish engineer John Rennie designed London Bridge, Waterloo Bridge and other crossings of the Thames.
